description: We are computer engineers from UPC
summary:
Mare Hackematis is a free web app that helps choose where to land on the Moon, using only official NASA data. Users choose a destination (South Pole, North Pole or the whole Moon), landing dates and mission priorities. The app then scores every location from 0 to 100 based on six factors: sunlight, Earth visibility for communications, slope, roughness, temperature and access to water ice.

A Python pipeline prepares LRO LOLA terrain, LRO Diviner temperatures, Lunar Prospector hydrogen and JPL SPICE ephemerides. For each 1 km cell at the poles and each 0.5° cell across the Moon, the browser then calculates hour by hour whether the Sun and the Earth rise above the real terrain horizon. It finds the best landing dates and highlights the top candidate sites, including the Artemis III regions. An Astronaut Mode lets users walk the terrain at real scale.

With Artemis returning humans to the lunar south pole, the app turns complex planetary datasets into clear, transparent decisions that anyone can explore and verify.
details:
Mare Hackematis started with a question that sounds simple. If you had to land on the Moon and stay there for two weeks, where would you go and when would you arrive? A site might get plenty of sunlight but have long periods when Earth is hidden behind the terrain. Another might offer better communications but be too steep for your mission. Our team, Hackemate, built a web app that lets people explore those trade-offs for themselves.

You start by choosing the South Pole, the North Pole, or the Whole Moon. Then you set your arrival date, how long you want to stay, and what matters most to your mission. At either pole, you can also give the app a range of dates and let it search for promising landing windows. The polar maps use one-kilometre cells for a closer look at the terrain. The global map gives you a broader view and compares sites for a fixed landing date.

The app uses lunar elevation data to work out how high the horizon is around each cell. It then checks when the Sun and Earth rise above that local horizon during the mission. Those results are combined with slope, roughness, temperature, and a water or ice indicator to produce a score out of 100. You choose how much each factor counts. You can also set limits, such as the steepest terrain your lander can handle, the longest time it can go without sunlight, or the minimum share of the mission with Earth in view.

Once you find an interesting spot, you can inspect the values behind its score, compare it with up to three other sites, or export the results. The maps also give you familiar places to start from, including published Artemis candidate regions, named northern craters, and the six Apollo landing sites. One of our favourite features is Astronaut Mode. You can go from looking at a point on the map to walking around it at real scale. Changing the time lets you see how the terrain affects what an astronaut would see, including whether a nearby ridge hides the Sun or Earth. The underlying landscape comes from lunar elevation data, and the interface identifies the small craters and rocks generated for the simulation.

We built the app with JavaScript, React, and Vite, using Three.js for the 3D views and Rapier for movement and physics. We processed the lunar datasets and prepared the Sun and Earth positions with Python, NumPy, SciPy, and SpiceyPy. The mission calculations run in the browser using Web Workers. We also used Claude and OpenAI Codex to help with development and writing.

A big part of the project was deciding what the data could reasonably tell us. For example, the polar model estimates where ice could remain stable, while the global resource layer uses hydrogen measurements as an indirect indicator. The South Pole map shows observed ice separately. We checked our polar visibility estimates against published LOLA maps and checked the Sun and Earth positions at selected southern sites against JPL Horizons. We hope the app helps mission teams build an initial shortlist and gives students and curious explorers a way to see how one change in a mission plan can lead to a different choice of landing site.
